sections.text: A shared reference only lets you read. To change a borrowed value, use a mutable reference: &mut. The variable itself must be declared mut.
The key rule: at any moment you can have either one mutable reference, or any number of shared references, but not both.
This rule stops one part of a program from changing data while another part is reading or changing it, which prevents a whole class of bugs called data races.
A borrow lasts until the last time it's used, not until the end of the block. That's why r2 is allowed after the last use of r.
Think of a whiteboard: many people can read it at once, or one person can write on it, but nobody should read while someone is halfway through writing.

exercise.prompt: Finish double so it doubles the number through the mutable reference (use *n). It should print: 42

tests.label: double turns 21 into 42
Calling double twice turns 3 into 12
zero stays zero
a negative number
other variables are not touched

hints: The parameter n is a reference, not a number. To change the value it points to, follow the reference first.
Use * to follow a reference, as in the lesson's *r += 5. Then do the doubling on the value behind it.
Inside double write *n = *n * 2; (or the shorter *n *= 2;, which works like +=).

quiz.question: How many mutable references to a value can be in use at once?
quiz.explanation: Only one mutable reference to a value can be in use at a time. This rule stops two parts of the program from changing the same data at once.

quiz.question: Can you have a &mut and a & to the same value in use at the same time?
quiz.explanation: While a &mut is in use, no & to the same value can be in use, because the reader might see data change underneath it. This is true for every type, numbers included.

quiz.question: What does the dereference operator * do in *r += 1?
options: Follows the reference to change the value it points to
quiz.explanation: * dereferences: it follows the reference to the value it points at, so *r += 1 changes that value. It isn't multiplication here, and it doesn't change whether r itself is mutable.
